source_text: Ac per hoc et tibi vehementer obnixa est, dicens, non omnes fingi in condemnationem, in quam tu omnes ire pronuntias. Absurdissime autem argumentari soles, ut dicas: Sed hi non finguntur in condemnationem, qui postea liberantur; cum nec sic possit sermonis apostolici tibi vel superficies convenire. Nam cum dicis tu: Omnes in condemnationem creantur lege nascendi, sed aliqui inde, licet perexigui, mysteriis liberantur; non hoc asseris quod ille, qui non solum de condemnatis liberari praedicat, verum non omnes in condemnationem fingi, sed alios in contumeliam, alios in honorem.
pass_a_gloss: And through this it is also vehemently opposed to you, saying, that not all are fashioned into condemnation, into which you pronounce all go. But most absurdly you are accustomed to argue, that you say: But these are not fashioned into condemnation, who afterward are freed; when not even so can the surface of the apostolic speech even fit you. For when you say: All are created into condemnation by the law of being born, but some from there, though very tiny, are freed by the mysteries; you do not assert this which he, who not only preaches that from the condemned they are freed, but that not all are fashioned into condemnation, but others unto insult, others unto honor.
pass_b_english: Consequently, it strongly opposed you too by saying that not everyone is formed for the condemnation into which you declare everyone goes. You habitually make the utterly absurd argument: “But those who are afterward freed are not formed for condemnation.” Yet not even the surface of the apostle's words can agree with you in that way. When you say, “Everyone is created for condemnation by the law of birth, but some, though very few, are freed from it through the mysteries”, you do not assert what he does. He proclaims not only that people are freed from among the condemned, but that not everyone is formed for condemnation: some are formed for dishonor, others for honor.

choices.why: Paul in Julian's citations; keep Apostle not 'Paul' unless Paulus is written.
Julian means Scripture's legal/authoritative witness, especially the divine Law as teacher of justice.
rejected: natural law (unless the sentence is philosophical)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
